messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 65
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Prosecutor
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 65

# Case Vignette: Robert

Robert is a 65-year-old married man who has spent the better part of four decades as a prosecutor, a career built on the conviction that the law, applied faithfully, is a force for protection. He is the kind of man who chooses his words carefully, who trusts in procedure, and who has always believed that institutions, however imperfect, hold. That belief began to fracture two years ago on a Tuesday afternoon in a parking garage downtown, and it has not fully recovered since.

He had been walking to his car after a late hearing when he witnessed two officers beating a young Black man who had already been restrained on the ground. The blows were unhurried and methodical, and what Robert remembers most is not the sound — though the sound stays with him — but the officers' faces, which were calm. He stood frozen behind a concrete pillar, briefcase in hand, watching something he had spent his career insisting could not happen this way, not like this, not without consequence. He did not intervene. He told himself afterward that it would have made things worse. He is still not sure he believes that.

In the weeks that followed, Robert found himself unable to sleep past three in the morning. He would lie beside his wife Carol, eyes open, replaying the sequence of events with the same prosecutorial precision he brings to a case — searching for the moment he could have acted differently, for the procedural failure, for the point at which order might have been restored. There is never a satisfying answer. His mind simply runs the footage again.

At work, things have become complicated in ways he struggles to articulate to his colleagues. He sits across from police officers every day, depends on them for testimony, coordinates with them on cases. He knows, intellectually, that the men he works with are not the men in the garage. But when a uniformed officer enters his office and closes the door, something in his chest tightens in a way that does not respond to reason. He has begun scheduling those meetings with the door left open. No one has commented on it yet.

He has stopped using that parking garage. He takes a longer route to his car now, adding fifteen minutes to his commute, and he cannot fully explain this to Carol, who has noticed the change in him but not yet named it. He is short with her in the evenings in ways that shame him. He finds himself drinking two glasses of scotch where he used to drink one, not for pleasure but to dull the particular alertness that settles over him after dark.

What disturbs Robert most is not the nightmares, though those come reliably — the concrete floor, the sound, the calm faces — but rather the way the experience has begun to corrode his sense of professional identity. He is a man who built his life on the premise that bearing witness to wrongdoing obligates a response. He has prosecuted people for doing exactly what he did: standing by. The cognitive dissonance of this is not abstract for him. It surfaces in the middle of closing arguments, in the pause before he calls his next witness, in the moment he catches his own reflection in the darkened window of a courtroom at dusk.

He describes himself as someone who used to feel certain. Not arrogant — he is careful to make that distinction — but grounded. He knew what he stood for. Now he sits in his office surrounded by forty years of case files and commendations and finds himself wondering whether he has ever understood the system he has served as well as he believed he did. That uncertainty, quiet and persistent, follows him home each evening, sits with him through dinner, and is still there when he wakes at three in the morning and cannot find his way back to sleep.
